title: Proving the Limited Scalability of Centralized Distributed Optimization via a New Lower Bound Construction
claim: A smooth, carefully shaped hard-instance function and its derivatives have bounded, controlled behavior, forming the building block of the lower-bound construction.
layout: 2x2 grid of line plots; function above derivative, left family and right single curve
description: Four line plots in a 2x2 grid. The top-left plot shows a family of functions Ψ_e (orange dashed), Ψ_1.15 (green dash-dot) and Ψ_1.04 (red dotted). Each is zero until about x=0.55 to 0.75, then rises smoothly to cross 1 at x=1 and flattens toward a plateau, with y-ticks at 1 and e. The bottom-left plot shows their derivatives Ψ′ as bump-shaped curves. The red one is a tall narrow spike near 0.58, the green one is a medium peak near 0.65, and the orange one is a wide low hump near 0.9. A y-tick marks √(54/e). The right column shows Γ (purple), which decreases from 2 at x=-1.5 to 0 near x=-0.25 and stays zero. Below it, Γ′ rises from about -e to 0 near x=-0.1. All plots have grids and legends. The eye goes first to the colorful curve families on the left.

abstract: We consider centralized distributed optimization in the classical federated learning setup, where $n$ workers jointly find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of an $L$-smooth, $d$-dimensional nonconvex function $f$, having access only to unbiased stochastic gradients with variance $Ï^2$. Each worker requires at most $h$ seconds to compute a stochastic gradient, and the communication times from the server to the workers and from the workers to the server are $Ï_{s}$ and $Ï_{w}$ seconds per coordinate, respectively. One of the main motivations for distributed optimization is to achieve scalability with respect to $n$. For instance, it is well known that the distributed version of SGD has a variance-dependent runtime term $\frac{h Ï^2 L Î}{n \varepsilon^2},$ which improves with the number of workers $n,$ where $Î= f(x^0) - f^*,$ and $x^0 \in R^d$ is the starting point. Similarly, using unbiased sparsification compressors, it is possible to reduce both the variance-dependent runtime term and the communication runtime term. However, once we account for the communication from the server to the workers $Ï_{s}$, we prove that it becomes infeasible to design a method using unbiased random sparsification compressors that scales both the server-side communication runtime term $Ï_{s} d \frac{L Î}{\varepsilon}$ and the variance-dependent runtime term $\frac{h Ï^2 L Î}{\varepsilon^2},$ better than poly-logarithmically in $n$, even in the homogeneous (i.i.d.) case, where all workers access the same distribution. To establish this result, we construct a new "worst-case" function and develop a new lower bound framework that reduces the analysis to the concentration of a random sum, for which we prove a concentration bound. These results reveal fundamental limitations in scaling distributed optimization, even under the homogeneous assumption.
